title: How to create a bootable macOS USB installer for macOS 27 Golden Gate and older
content:
Macworld





Being able to create a bootable USB installer for macOS is a useful skill for any Mac user. Whether you’re performing a clean install, setting up multiple Macs, recovering a system that won’t boot, or simply want a reliable offline installer, a bootable USB drive gives you far more control than relying on macOS Recovery alone.
Creating a bootable installer is easier than it used to be thanks to Apple’s Terminal command, createinstallmedia, but the process still isn’t obvious – and it differs depending on whether you’re using an Intel Mac or a Mac with Apple silicon. You’ll need the correct macOS installer, a USB drive with enough capacity, and a few Terminal commands that need to be entered exactly.
In this guide, we’ll show you how to create a bootable USB installer for macOS Golden Gate, as well as macOS Tahoe, macOS Sequoia and older versions of macOS. We’ll explain what you need before you begin, how the process differs between Intel and Apple silicon Macs, and how to use your installer once it’s ready. By the end, you’ll have a reusable macOS installer that can save you time, bandwidth and frustration – and it might even help you recover a Mac when nothing else will.

PROMOTION
Create a bootable installer on Mac FREE




EaseUS Data Recovery Wizard for Mac is not only a hard drive recovery tool on macOS devices but also a bootable installer creator. Just with a click, it clones the boot disk to create a bootable USB and gets your macOS updated or boot from the installer. Also this bootable disk manager helps to install macOS, perform system repairs, or even reinstall the operating system on the go.
Free Trial

Buy and Save 25%




We also explain how to create a bootable installer for the latest macOS beta, where available, and provide instructions for macOS Golden Gate, Tahoe, Sequoia and earlier releases.
Why create a bootable USB mac installer
Creating a bootable USB macOS installer is a versatile tool for troubleshooting, system maintenance, and managing multiple computers.
There are several specific scenarios where a bootable USB is superior to standard software updates or built-in Recovery modes:
Clean Installations and Troubleshooting: A bootable drive allows you to wipe a Mac’s internal storage and install a fresh copy of the operating system. This is often the best way to fix persistent software issues, resolve persistent software problems, or prepare a machine for a new owner. See: How to do a clean install of macOS
Installing on Multiple Macs: Instead of downloading the multi-gigabyte installer (which can be 16GB or more) on every individual machine, you can download it once and use the USB to update several Macs quickly.
Installing on a separate volume: You can also use your bootable installer to install macOS on a separate volume of your hard drive.
Beta updates: Installing the latest macOS beta
Downgrading macOS: If a new update like macOS Golden Gate causes issues, a bootable installer is the primary method for rolling back to a previous version like macOS Tahoe. See: How to downgrade macOS update and rollback to the previous version and How to get older versions of macOS.
Unsupported Hardware: For users with older Intel-based Macs that Apple no longer officially supports, a bootable USB can be required to use tools like the OpenCore Legacy Patcher to install newer versions of macOS.
Emergency Access: If your Mac can’t access Recovery mode. 


SpeedFaster than downloading the OS via Recovery mode for every install.
Reduced downloadingThe macOS installer is stored on the drive, so you don’t need to download the full OS on every Mac. An internet connection may still be required during installation.
VersatilitySupports clean installs, downgrades, and patching unsupported Macs.
EfficiencyOne drive can update an entire fleet of Mac computers.

 






How to create a bootable macOS Installer 
We will run through the following steps to create a bootable USB for Mac:
Get the macOS installer files
Create a bootable installer for macOS
Choose the correct createinstallmedia command
What you need to make a bootable USB for Mac
A 32GB Flash Drive (Minimum): To create a bootable USB installer, you typically need a USB flash drive or Thunderbolt drive with at least 16GB (we recommend 32GB) of space. Using a faster drive, such as a USB 3.0 or USB-C stick, is recommended to reduce installation times. 

Note: If you have data on the drive that you plan to use you will need to transfer it to another drive, as it will be completely formatted and erased.
macOS installation files: You can obtain these from the Mac App Store, Software Update in System Settings, or other official Apple sources.
A Compatible Mac.
Admin access: You will need to have an admin user account on the Mac you are working with. 
Internet access: It goes without saying that you will need an internet connection to download the software and you may need it while installing the version of macOS if it needs to check for firmware or confirm your iCloud credentials.


						

							






						

							
1.
Get the macOS installer files

				
					

				
			
You can get installers from the Mac App Store – as long as your Mac is compatible.

Foundry






How you get the installation files will depend on the version you want the installer for. Below we’ll look at how to get various macOS installers. If it’s an older version you are after, we have a dedicated article about How to download old Mac OS X and macOS versions.
Warning: Download the installation files, but make sure you stop before the actual installation starts. When the installation starts the files will be disposed of, so you need to step in beforehand!
Where to get macOS Golden Gate installer: From September 14, macOS Golden Gate can be downloaded on compatible Macs through the Software Update mechanism within macOS. Navigate to the Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update. Your Mac will check for the latest version, and you can click Upgrade Now to begin the download.
Where to get the macOS beta: To get the latest beta files you need to first register for the Apple’s official developer or public beta programs. You can then download the latest beta from Software Update, as described above. See: Latest macOS beta details and how to get it.
Where to get other macOS installers: You can download the installers from these Mac App Store links. Make sure you use Safari and close the Mac App Store before clicking on the link or it may not work. If your Mac is too new it may not be compatible with these older versions. 
macOS Tahoe
macOS Sequoia
macOS Sonoma
macOS Ventura
macOS Monterey
macOS Big Sur
macOS Catalina 
macOS Mojave
macOS High Sierra
Once the installation files are downloaded you will be able to find them in the Applications folder via the Finder. Now you have the installation files, we can move on to the process of making the bootable installer.
Creating a bootable installation of macOS requires a single command in Terminal (this has been the case since Mavericks arrived in 2013). The createinstallmedia command makes it possible to create a bootable copy of an installer on any drive that’s connected to your Mac. You’ll find all the createinstallmedia commands at the bottom of this article.
Warning: The createinstallmedia command erases anything on the external disk you use for your bootable drive, so make sure there’s nothing on it that you need.

						

							
2.
Connect and prepare the drive manually, if necessary

				
					

				
			
Using Disk Utility to prepare the hard drive. 

Foundry






You may not need to prepare the drive manually. If everything in step 3 (below) works as expected, the createinstallmedia command will erase the external drive and format it as Mac OS Extended (Journaled) automatically. You can therefore skip these Disk Utility steps and go straight to creating the bootable installer. However, if createinstallmedia can’t erase or prepare the drive correctly, we recommend formatting it manually first using the steps below.
Connect a USB flash drive or other external drive with at least 32GB of space. Everything on the drive will be erased, so make a copy of anything you want to keep first.
Open Disk Utility (press Command + spacebar and start to type Disk Utility).
In Disk Utility click View and select Show All Devices.
From the sidebar, physical external drive itself, rather than one of the volumes underneath it.
Click Erase.
Give the drive a simple name such as MyVolume. You can use another name, but you must use that exact name later in the Terminal command.
Set Scheme to GUID Partition Map. Note that createinstallmedia will ultimately erase the drive as Mac OS Extended (Journaled).
Click Erase, wait for Disk Utility to finish, then click Done. 

						

							
3.
Create the bootable macOS installer

				
					

				
			
Use Terminal to create your installer.

Foundry






Before starting this part of the process, make sure the full macOS installer is in your Applications folder. If you ran the update when you downloaded it the installer will need to be downloaded again. 
Open Terminal (Command + Space and type Terminal).
Enter the createinstallmedia command for the version of macOS you want to install. You can find the commands at the bottom of this article. 
Press Return.
Enter your administrator password when prompted. Nothing will appear on screen while you type the password; this is normal.
If macOS asks Terminal for permission to access the removable drive, click OK.
When Terminal warns that the drive will be erased, type Y and press Return.
Wait while Terminal erases the drive and copies the macOS installer. This may take several minutes. When it is finished you should see “Copy complete. Done.” 
The external drive is now a bootable macOS installer.

						

							
4.
Boot the Mac from the installer

				
					

				
			
Foundry






This process is different on Apple silicon and Intel Macs.
On an Apple Silicon Mac:
Connect the installer drive and shut down the Mac.
Press and hold the power button until Startup Options appears.
Select the macOS installer.
Click Continue.
On an Intel Mac:
Connect the installer drive and shut down the Mac.
Turn it on while holding the Option/Alt key.
Select the macOS installer from the startup menu.
Press Return or choose Continue.
Note: Apple warns that Macs with a T2 Security Chip may need Startup Security Utility configured to allow booting from external or removable media.

						

							
5.
Install macOS

				
					

				
			
Install the version of macOS you want.

Foundry






Once the Mac has started from the USB installer, choose the option to Install macOS and follow the onscreen instructions. 
The installer can only install that version of macOS on Macs that support it.
If you want a clean install, you must first erase the Mac’s internal disk before installing macOS; otherwise, you can install the OS normally without wiping the Mac. Read How to clean install macOS for step-by-step instructions.

						

							
createinstallmedia commands 
The createinstallmedia command will be slightly different depending on which version of macOS you are wanting to use.
Note MyVolume may have a different name for you, for example it might be USB or Untitled. Check in Disk Utilities, it’s the name of the external disk you are using.
WARNING: We have heard of people copying and pasting in the -- only for them to change to a – in Terminal, so be careful of that. There should be two dashes!
Golden Gate
sudo /Applications/Install\ macOS\ Golden\ Gate.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume
Tahoe 
sudo /Applications/Install\ macOS\ Tahoe.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume
Sequoia
sudo /Applications/Install\ macOS\ Sequoia.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume

Monterey

Big Sur 
sudo /Applications/Install\ macOS\ Big\ Sur.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume
Catalina
sudo /Applications/Install\ macOS\ Catalina.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume
Mojave
sudo /Applications/Install\ macOS\ Mojave.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume
High Sierra
sudo /Applications/Install\ macOS\ High\ Sierra.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume
Sierra
sudo /Applications/Install\ macOS\ Sierra.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume --applicationpath /Applications/Install\ macOS\ Sierra.app
El Capitan
sudo /Applications/Install\ OS\ X\ El\ Capitan.app/Contents/Resources/createinstallmedia --volume /Volumes/MyVolume --applicationpath /Applications/Install\ OS\ X\ El\ Capitan.app
Yosemite

title: Your old iPhone is actually going to get faster this week
content:
Macworld





The main highlight of iOS 27, launching on September 14, will be artificial intelligence, which is only available on relatively new phones (iPhone 15 Pro, and iPhone 16 and later). Head over to the iOS 27 site on Apple.com, and you’ll see a lot about the new Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, and other features that require the latest hardware to run. Unsurprisingly, this might leave owners of older iPhones wondering what exactly they’ll gain from the update.
After spending some time testing the iOS 27 beta on an iPhone 11 Pro Max (the oldest iPhone supported by the update), I can report that iOS 27 is just as important for older iPhones—maybe even more so. Although they’ll miss out on the latest AI features, iOS 27 may be the best update older iPhones have received in years.
iOS 27 makes older iPhones fast again
If you’ve installed iOS 26 on an older iPhone, you’ve probably noticed that some things weren’t exactly smooth. Even some of the latest iPhones had some trouble running the fancy animations added with Liquid Glass.
Earlier this year, I wrote about how iOS 26 seemed noticeably buggy compared to other recent iOS releases. Animations stuttered more often, apps took longer to launch, and even basic system interactions sometimes felt sluggish.
Apple promised that iOS 27 would address many of these issues. Even before the release candidate arrived this week, my tests with the iPhone 11 Pro Max show that the company was serious about improving performance, especially when it comes to old hardware.

				
					

				
			
iOS 27 will bring some design refinements to Liquid Glass, but the real improvements are with performance.

Foundry




To get a better idea of how much has changed, I measured the time it takes to complete a handful of common tasks on the same iPhone 11 Pro Max running iOS 26 and iOS 27 beta 1.
I started with something simple that most people do every day: taking photos with their iPhone. On iOS 26, my iPhone 11 took 0.98 seconds to open the Camera app, then 3.61 seconds to take a photo and load it into my photo library.
I ran the test again with iOS 27, and the improvements were noticeable. Now it only takes about 0.65 seconds to open the Camera app, and 2.44 seconds to take a photo and immediately open it from the thumbnail preview. For users, this means a lower chance of missing an important shot because their phone is too slow.
Many iPhone users also rely on the Maps app every day, and on iOS 26, the iPhone 11 took a long 3.01 seconds to load it. With the first beta of iOS 27, the same iPhone now loads the Maps app in just 1.36 seconds. That’s twice as fast as on iOS 26.
Other actions, such as launching Safari, browsing the App Store, and opening the share sheet, are also noticeably faster in iOS 27. 

iOS 27 beta vs. iOS 26 speed tests

		
			


Results are in seconds. Lower results/shorter bars are better.




On their own, these numbers won’t transform the experience. After all, we’re talking about fractions of a second in some cases. But when you’re running these tasks multiple times a day, every second adds up to minutes saved. And the whole system feels remarkably faster.
The smoother animations matter even more
Performance benchmarks are only part of the story. What really makes iOS 27 better on the iPhone 11 is how much smoother the animations feel during everyday use.
Visuals everywhere appear more consistent and less prone to frame drops. Swiping to open Control Center is noticeably more fluid. Unlocking the phone feels more responsive. App transitions seem better optimized and less likely to hitch. 
Those were all things that bothered me when I tried using this iPhone on iOS 26, and now Apple seems to have fixed nearly all of the slow animations.
Once again, these aren’t dramatic changes individually, but together they create the impression that the old hardware is no longer struggling to keep up with the operating system. The result is an iPhone that feels newer than it actually is.

				
					

				
			
You won’t get all of the features that you get on the iPhone 17 PRI Max, but iOS 27 will still be an impressive upgrade for older iPhones.

Foundry




iOS 27 also runs cooler
Another change I noticed almost immediately is the temperature. While my iPhone 11 Pro Max heats up quite easily on iOS 26, even when performing basic tasks, iOS 27 seems to keep the phone cool for longer. And that’s a great sign that the optimizations Apple made across the system have worked.
A cooler phone generally indicates that software processes are being managed more efficiently. It often means less unnecessary CPU and GPU activity, which can also translate into better battery life over time.
What’s more, these numbers were from one of the earlier betas, so it’s likely that the version Apple ships Monday will be even better for battery life.
Older iPhones are getting a lot
If you watched the WWDC keynote, you might have been disappointed, as it seemed as though older iPhones wouldn’t be getting anything more than bug fixes with iOS 27. But that’s not actually the case. In fact, while devices like the iPhone 11 won’t support Siri AI, there are still many other new features coming to these devices.
One of my favorite new features in iOS 27 is the new clipboard shortcut right on the keyboard, which makes it faster to paste text or even a screenshot you just took. Being able to control the volume of the alarms and timers independently was also a nice addition.

				
					

				
			
Older iPhones won’t miss out on small iOS 27 features like this clipboard upgrade in the keyboard.

Foundry




There’s also the ability to create custom passes in the Wallet app, a redesigned interface that makes it easier to play audio messages in iMessage, an option to save a high-resolution frame from a video in the Photos app, and larger Home Screen widgets.
All of these features are coming to older iPhones with iOS 27. Sure, they might not sound as exciting as a new AI assistant that can control your phone, but they’re exactly the kind of improvements that make your phone feel more useful and polished.
Not to mention that all iPhones getting iOS 27 will feature refinements to the Liquid Glass interface, including the new transparency slider that lets you choose the look you want.
iOS 27 is a surprisingly great update for aging iPhones
To be honest, I was quite surprised when Apple confirmed that even the iPhone 11 would get the iOS 27 update. After all, my experience running iOS 26 on that generation of phone was quite frustrating. But now that I’ve tried the first beta, I can see why Apple made that decision.
The main narrative surrounding iOS 27 focuses heavily on AI, and that’s completely understandable. Apple had been lagging behind in this race, so it’s no surprise that they want to make a big deal out of all the new Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features.

				
					

				
			
Don’t worry about missing out on Siri AI. iOS 27 is a fantastic upgrade for older iPhones.

Foundry




Yet, after using iOS 27 on an iPhone 11 Pro Max, I can’t help but think that older devices may be among the biggest beneficiaries of this update. The software feels faster. Animations are smoother. The phone runs cooler. And users still get a collection of useful new features despite missing out on AI.
For anyone worried that iOS 27 would leave older iPhones behind, the first beta suggests the opposite. Apple appears to have spent just as much time optimizing the experience for existing users as it did building features for future hardware, and that’s great news for people still holding onto a seven-year-old iPhone.

title: Apple apparently doesn’t want you hanging out at its stores anymore
content:
Macworld





The reign of new CEO John Ternus has only just got underway, but Apple is already plotting a major revamp to its retail strategy.
According to the latest instalment of Mark Gurman’s Power On newsletter, the company is preparing a “retail store shake-up” that will see its brick-and-mortar outlets shift focus from so-called “community landmarks” and gathering places towards “more traditional and practical” retail spaces. The priority, it would appear, will be on encouraging customers to buy rather than to connect with the community.
The revamp will feature three major changes, Gurman describes. Dedicated Genius Bars will return. The giant video walls currently found in some outlets will vanish. And the “Avenue” sections along the sides of Apple stores will be redesigned and repurposed for collection of online purchases and hosting “Today at Apple” workshops. New fixtures for the Genius Bars and redesigned Avenues will be made entirely from wood, Gurman reports, while looking “fully integrated–as if they had been part of the original design.”
The presence of Genius Bars and the continuation of Today at Apple sessions indicates that the company hasn’t completely given up on its strategy of encouraging customers to visit for reasons other than making a purchase. But such hosting, helping, and community functions are reportedly set to become a lower priority, in stark contrast to the Apple store’s founding principles.
 It isn’t clear why Apple wants to move in a different direction now. In 2001 Ron Johnson envisaged the stores as hubs for the Apple user community, and he even modelled early examples on public buildings such as libraries, rather than rival shops. Angela Ahrendts and Jony Ive later evolved the concept as a high-concept luxury space and statement of the company’s aesthetic values: a town hall for likeminded people. This was a risky and unusual approach, but it paid off. (Johnson’s and Ahrendts’ retail efforts each landed them spots in our rundown of the 50 most important people in Apple’s history.) 
Gurman adds that Apple is bringing in stricter rules for its retail employees, who have complained about conditions in the past and may be surprised to hear that stricter rules are necessary. Staff will be required to stand throughout pre-opening meetings, he says, and will be forbidden from drinking or looking at devices, and must “stay fully engaged.” When doors open, every staff member will be required to applaud the first customers. It’s debatable whether they will be in the mood to applaud after hearing about the new rules.

title: Apple Stores Said to Lose Video Walls, Regain Dedicated Genius Bars
content:
Apple is working on a sweeping retail overhaul that would bring back dedicated Genius Bars to its stores, carve out new spaces for order pickup and Today at Apple classes, and do away with oversized video walls, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


In this week's "Power On" newsletter, Gurman said that Apple intends to speed up store renovations over the coming years. Apple plans to rework the "Avenue," its term for the side sections of a store where accessories and services are displayed, reinstate standalone Genius Bars, and remove the large video screens installed in many locations.

Pickup and Today at Apple, which typically share a counter and a seating area today, will each get their own compact section along the Avenue, described internally as a "bay" and measuring about 10 feet across.

For pickup, Gurman described plans for an all-wood bay with a faint Apple logo worked into the upper section, with lockable drawers underneath for holding customer orders, fronted by a counter where staff can hand items over. The Today at Apple bay will feature a similar look, topped by a display similar to a large television, with drawers below for stashing iPads, laptops, and other class equipment, plus a fixed instructor table and stools nearby.

The video walls being phased out trace back to the retail vision pursued under former retail chief Angela Ahrendts, who treated Apple stores as public gathering places rather than purely transactional spaces. Gurman frames the current shift as a move away from that toward stores built primarily around service, fulfillment, and everyday shopping needs.

Where those screens come down, most stores will gain a wood finished Genius Bar built to echo the design Apple used before it introduced the open plan "Genius Grove." It includes counters set at two different heights for accessibility, backed by a wall of storage drawers and large product imagery. Gurman added that both the new bars and the Avenue bays are meant to look as though they always belonged in the store, rather than as visible retrofits, and that many renovated locations will also see their break rooms and other back-of-house areas refurbished.

Elements of the redesign are already live in a small number of stores around the world. Gurman expects the fuller version of the proposed store overhaul to reach most newly opened and renovated stores gradually, with the international rollout continuing over several years.
